channel.title: Server Roles: Windows and Linux :: School-related IT Infrastructure
channel.description: Sessions: 16.11.2026 and 23.11.2026 · Documentation technique: Runbooks · Role runbook due: 06.12.2026 A school network needs more than cables and addresses. Devices get their address automatically, names are resolved, teachers log in with one account on every computer, find their class folders, print, open the school website, and in summer 25 computer-lab PCs are set up again in one hour. Each of these tasks is a server role. In this chapter you build, over two sessions, a working school network together out of eight server roles, and you build it twice:

item.title: Learning goals
item.description: After these two sessions you can: explain what a server role is, and describe each of the eight roles of a school network (DHCP, DNS, directory service, file shares, printing, web, client deployment, remote access) with an example from everyday school life, set up, test and undo one role in the Windows world (Windows Server 2025, preferably with PowerShell) and in the Linux world (Debian 13, free software), prove with acceptance tests from a test client that a role works from the users’ point of view, name the dependencies between the roles (no directory service without DNS, no domain accounts for shares, printers and remote access without a directory service) and narrow down faults along this chain, combine the Windows and Linux worlds (e.g. a Linux client on Active Directory, a Windows client on a Samba share) and explain which open protocols make this work (DHCP, DNS, LDAP, Kerberos, SMB, IPP, HTTP, PXE), compare both solutions of a role with reasons: licence costs, operating effort, vendor dependence, further development, data protection and suitability for support by a team of teachers, document your own work as a role runbook, with copyable commands and a column for undoing each step, explain your own role in a short presentation to others who did not build it themselves. Mapping to the competency list: to follow (placeholder).

item.title: Access to the Proxmox lab
item.description: All servers and test clients of this chapter run on the lecturer’s Proxmox VE server. Proxmox itself is an example of the Linux world: a free hypervisor based on Debian that manages virtual machines (VMs) and Linux containers (LXC) (see chapter 1). Logging in You get the address of the Proxmox web interface and your credentials in the session. When logging in, choose Proxmox VE authentication server as the realm. In the tree on the left you see only the machines of your team (pool pool-team<N>) and the two test clients. Console only The lab VLAN is not reachable from the university network. So you cannot connect from your laptop via SSH or Remote Desktop. Everything runs through the console in the Proxmox web interface, and all tests run inside the lab. For tests “from outside”, use the test clients or a machine of another team.

item.title: Role cards
item.description: Each role card describes what has to run at the end, not how every click looks. You find the way there as a team with the official documentation (section Entry points). Exactly this way is what you record in the role runbook: a runbook that is only copied from the book helps nobody in an emergency. Every card has the same sections: Section Content The role at a school What the role is for, with an example from everyday school life Dependencies Which other roles have to run first Goal in the Windows world / Goal in the Linux world What runs at the end of session 1 (on its own, without a domain) Goal in session 2 How the role works together with the others Acceptance tests How you prove from the test client that it works Pitfalls What usually goes wrong Entry points Official documentation (primary sources) Comparison questions Questions for the runbook and the presentation Status: untested The commands, package names and menu items on the role cards have not yet been run in the Proxmox lab. Software as of November 2026 (Windows Server 2025, Debian 13 “trixie”). Check versions and commands in the official documentation. Tested on: open.

item.title: Integration (session 2)
item.description: When: 23.11.2026, 08:45–11:15 · Who: all teams, in the order below In session 1 each team built its role on its own. Now the roles should work together: the test clients get the DNS server of their domain via DHCP, log in with domain accounts, connect shares and printers and boot from the network. This only works in the right order, because every role waits for others. This page is the shared plan for the room. The details for each role are on the role cards in the section Goal in session 2.

item.title: Documentation task: role runbook
item.description: Technique Read first in the documentation script: Runbooks Graded The role runbook is the graded portfolio entry of this chapter (rubric see assessment). Due: 06.12.2026. There is no separate homework in this chapter. Task Each role team writes one shared runbook for its role. It describes how to set up, check and undo the role in the Windows world and in the Linux world, so that another team of teachers can rebuild it without asking. The runbook is in the portfolios of all team members (same file). In addition, each person writes a short personal reflection.

item.title: Role presentation
item.description: Required, not graded The role presentation is required but not graded. Its purpose is to show the others what you built. Only the role runbook is graded. When: 23.11.2026, 11:30–12:30 · Duration: 6 minutes per team, then changeover · Audience: all other teams, who did not build your role What goes into the six minutes Minute Content 1 The role at a school in two sentences, with an example from everyday school life 2–4 Live or as screenshots: an acceptance test in the Windows world and the same test in the Linux world, from the test client 5 One combination of Windows and Linux that worked (or why not) 6 Comparison and recommendation: one slide or table with effort, costs, vendor dependence. Which world would you recommend to Mittelschule Musterstadt? Tips Live demos in the Proxmox lab are welcome. Still keep screenshots ready in case something fails at exactly that moment. Whoever is not speaking operates the console. How you split up is your team’s decision. Do not show long lists of commands; those are in the runbook. Show the result. One slide is enough. Anything that can be shown in the classroom is allowed, including your README in the browser. For the audience Note one question or observation per role. At the end we collect together: where did Linux have the advantage, where Windows, and where did it not matter? The result is the starting point for session 5 (device management) and for the architecture decision in the capstone project.

item.title: Demo: certificate services
item.description: When: 23.11.2026, approx. 15 min within the 10:30–11:15 block · Who: lecturer (demonstration), for everyone to read afterwards · Machines: 10.50.13.18 (Windows), 10.50.13.29 (Linux) Demonstration, not a team task Certificate services are not a team’s role. Your own certificate authority is hard to undo (see below) and depends on the directory service. That is why the lecturer shows it once in each world. Status: untested The commands have not yet been run in the Proxmox lab. Tested on: open.

item.title: Security and data protection
item.description: No legal advice This section gives technical orientation. Legal questions (e.g. legal basis, retention periods, data processing agreements) are clarified by the school with the data protection officer and the school maintainer. The essentials Topic Measure Few administrator accounts A normal account for daily work, a separate administrator account for administration. The domain administrator is used only for domain tasks. One service, one server Each role on its own server or container: a fault in or attack on the web server does not immediately reach the domain controller. This is exactly how the lab is built. Only necessary services What is not needed is not installed. Server Core and minimal Debian installations have a smaller attack surface. Updates Update servers regularly, in the lab too. Debian: unattended-upgrades for security updates. Windows: Windows Update. Remote access Never Remote Desktop or SSH directly from the internet. SSH with keys, Remote Desktop with NLA, from outside only via VPN with multi-factor login. Open resolvers and DHCP DNS answers recursive queries only from your own network. Only one planned DHCP server per network; rogue DHCP servers are blocked on the switch (DHCP snooping). Encryption Websites only with HTTPS. Internal certificates from your own certificate authority instead of clicking browser warnings away. SMB1 stays switched off. Backup Domain controllers, shares and configuration files are backed up, and restoring is practised. A snapshot is not a backup. Data protection in the school context Directory service: it contains names, class membership, login times and groups of minors. This belongs in the record of processing activities (see documentation script). Logs: DHCP (which device was on the network when), DNS (which sites are visited), print server (who prints what) and remote access (who logs in when) generate personal logs. Decide who may see them and when they are deleted. Own server or cloud: for roles in the cloud (Entra ID, Universal Print, Autopilot), the data is with a provider. That requires a data processing agreement and a check of where the data is processed. With your own servers, the school is responsible for operation and security itself. Images (team 7): a disk image can contain data of the last person who used the reference machine. Never use the reference machine with real accounts. Wipe old disks securely before passing them on. Test data: in the lab only made-up names (lehrer01, schueler01). No real class lists.
